questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of a saturated solution at a given temperature?
questions.a: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature; any additional solute added will not dissolve and will remain as a visible solid. A wrong answer (e.g., "a solution with a lot of solute" or "a concentrated solution") reveals the student confuses saturation with concentration — a solution can be concentrated but still unsaturated if more solute can dissolve.

questions.q: You have two beakers of salt water at room temperature. In Beaker A, a pinch of salt added dissolves completely. In Beaker B, the same pinch of salt sinks to the bottom unchanged. Which beaker contains a saturated solution and why?
questions.a: Beaker B contains the saturated solution because the added salt cannot dissolve — the solution already holds the maximum dissolved salt at that temperature. Beaker A is unsaturated because it can still accept more solute. A wrong answer (e.g., guessing Beaker A is saturated because it "looks saltier") shows the student relies on appearance rather than the operational test of adding solute.

questions.q: A student prepares a saturated solution of potassium nitrate (KNO₃) in 100 g of water at 40°C. The solubility of KNO₃ at 40°C is 64 g per 100 g water. The student then cools the solution to 20°C, where solubility is 32 g per 100 g water. How many grams of KNO₃ will crystallise out? (Assume no evaporation.)
questions.a: Step 1: At 40°C, maximum dissolved KNO₃ = 64 g in 100 g water. Step 2: At 20°C, maximum dissolved KNO₃ = 32 g in 100 g water. Step 3: Excess solute = 64 g − 32 g = 32 g. Step 4: This excess crystallises out upon cooling. Answer: 32 g of KNO₃ crystallises. A wrong answer (e.g., 64 g or 0 g) reveals the student does not connect solubility change with temperature or misunderstands that the "lost" dissolved solute becomes solid crystals.

questions.q: Two students test different solutions for saturation by adding a single crystal of the same solute. Student X observes the crystal dissolves completely. Student Y observes the crystal grows larger. Compare the saturation states of the two solutions and explain the crystal growth in Student Y's beaker.
questions.a: Student X's solution is unsaturated (crystal dissolves). Student Y's solution is saturated (crystal grows). The crystal grows because in a saturated solution, the rate of crystallisation equals the rate of dissolution; adding a seed crystal provides a surface for excess solute molecules to deposit, shifting the dynamic equilibrium toward net crystallisation. A wrong answer (e.g., "the crystal grew because the solution was unsaturated") shows the student does not understand dynamic equilibrium at saturation.

questions.q: A teacher claims: "If you heat a saturated solution, it will always become unsaturated." Evaluate this statement. Is it always true? Give a reason.
questions.a: The statement is generally true for most solid solutes (like salt, sugar) because solubility of solids usually increases with temperature, so heating a saturated solution raises its capacity to hold solute, making it unsaturated. However, it is NOT universally true — for some salts (e.g., cerium sulfate) solubility decreases with temperature, so heating could cause crystallisation. A wrong evaluation (e.g., "always true because heat makes things dissolve faster") reveals the student confuses rate of dissolving with equilibrium solubility, and ignores exceptions.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using only household items (sugar, salt, water, glasses, spoon, refrigerator, stove) to demonstrate that a saturated solution at room temperature becomes unsaturated when heated, and becomes supersaturated (with crystals forming) when cooled. Write the steps clearly.
questions.a: A good answer includes: (1) Make saturated sugar solution at room temp by adding sugar until no more dissolves. (2) Divide into two glasses. (3) Heat one glass gently — observe no crystals, solution becomes unsaturated (can add more sugar). (4) Cool the other glass in refrigerator — observe sugar crystals forming (supersaturation then crystallisation). (5) Explain each observation using solubility-temperature relationship. A poor answer (e.g., just "heat and cool") reveals the student cannot translate the concept into a testable procedure or identify the control variables.
